bib.title: Chapter 14: Data Analysis Examples (Python for Data Analysis, 2nd ed.)

question: How do the book's pandas, NumPy and matplotlib/seaborn techniques combine on five real datasets (Bitly 1.USA.gov, MovieLens 1M, SSA baby names, USDA food, FEC 2012)?
contributions: Five worked analyses: time-zone/OS counts, rating differences by gender, naming trends and diversity, nutrient lookup, campaign donations by occupation/size/state.

limits: Pandas version is 0.20-era (book dated 2017); several calls are dated: Int64Index in info output, pd.value_counts, rename(copy=False), groupby().apply returning the group keys, positional sum(1), chained assignment cframe['os']=..., pd.read_table(sep='::') without engine. Dated-API notes are the extractor's annotation, not stated in the chapter.
Data sources moved: the Bitly feed is shut down (stated), the SSA URL may have moved (stated); book supplies copies in its GitHub repo.
Chapter's printed output is not fully self-consistent: occ_mapping maps 'C.E.O.' to 'CEO', yet Out[208] still lists 'C.E.O.' for Romney while Out[203] shows CEO.
The code that stacks USDA nutrients (loop plus concat, In [166]) is absent from the extracted text between 'concatenated together with concat:' and 'If all goes well'.

Authors concede simplifications: Gary Johnson counted as Republican, 250-rating threshold arbitrary, Windows detected by substring, top-two bins excluded as non-individual donors, donors not de-duplicated by name/zip.
No inference, tests or uncertainty: all comparisons are descriptive; the diversity hypothesis is 'explored and confirmed' by plot only.
practices: Handle missing keys in JSON records with 'if key in rec' in the comprehension (14.1).
Prefer collections.Counter or Series.value_counts to hand-rolled count dicts (14.1).
Use fillna for NaN and boolean indexing for empty strings when labelling unknown categories (14.1).
Use nlargest instead of argsort/take for top-n (14.1).
Normalise within groups with groupby().transform('sum') rather than apply with a function (14.1).
Merge multi-table data into one frame first (pd.merge chain on overlapping names), then pivot_table (14.2).
Filter to groups with a minimum count before ranking group means (14.2).
Sanity-check group-derived columns, e.g. prop sums to 1 within each (year, sex) (14.3).
Assemble per-year files with a loop of read_csv, adding a year column, then concat(ignore_index=True) (14.3).
Use cumsum + searchsorted for 'how many items to reach q of the total' (14.3).
Drop duplicates and rename colliding column names before merging (14.4).
Use dict.get(x, x) in map so unmapped values pass through when cleaning categories (14.5).
Restrict to positive amounts before analysing contributions, since refunds are negative (14.5).
Discretise amounts with pd.cut and compare groups after normalising within buckets (14.5).
